content: To effectively implement a Public-Private Mix (PPM) strategy, it is essential to define sub-objectives and activities under each strategic objective. These include: 1. PPM Leadership and Stewardship: Identify which groups should convene and at what levels. Since most PPM implementation occurs at sub-national levels, governance at these levels, including input from civil society organizations, must not be overlooked. For each group, determine their core responsibilities, required actions, membership composition, meeting frequency, and expected outcomes. Assess the capacity-building efforts needed, including pre-service and in-service training for providers, as well as institutional capacity building for organizations delivering PPM services (e.g., professional associations and NGOs). Local PPM leadership groups should also be empowered to create localized roadmaps for PPM. Outline actions to enhance resource mobilization for PPM. 2. PPM Regulation: Evaluate the human resources and mechanisms required to strengthen regulatory systems, such as facility licensing, provider certification, facility accreditation, mandatory tuberculosis (TB) notification, regulation of TB antibiotic dispensing, and mandatory use of prescriptions for antibiotics. Explore whether medical councils or provider associations can aid in disseminating and enforcing these regulations. 3. Engaging Specific Facility and Provider Types: Develop a plan for mapping, documenting, and updating provider information at the local level, potentially including GPS mapping of facilities. Establish methods for recording and reporting provider referrals and notifications. Determine whether a simple electronic system exists for private providers to record and report data. If not, identify actions to develop such a system. Set targets for the number of facilities engaged, trained, and adopting key practices, revisiting these targets as necessary. Identify institutional capacity-building needs for implementing organizations, including resource mobilization efforts. Specify the tools, monitoring, and evaluation efforts required for each implementing organization. Consider incentives and enablers to support engagement. 4. PPM Monitoring and Evaluation: Define how mapping and notification data will be summarized and captured at higher levels of the health system. Plan for analyses of PPM data at each level of the health system, including cost per case diagnosed in different models, and determine the frequency of these assessments. 5. PPM Financing: Develop approaches to secure a greater share of donor TB financing for PPM. Explore how TB can be integrated into existing and new insurance initiatives, leveraging reimbursements to engage private providers in delivering quality TB care. For each of these areas, the consultation group should discuss the necessary actions, whether the next step involves a detailed assessment, development of a new system or methodology, or immediate rollout of an existing model. Additionally, the group should identify the human and financial resources required for these actions and potential sources for these resources. It is critical to assign ownership of each major area of work to an organization capable of recruiting and organizing the necessary staff to implement the outlined activities and achieve expansion targets. The national PPM action plan should include SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound) targets for each strategic objective, sub-objective, and activity. The plan should also include a comprehensive analysis of how it will contribute to closing the national gap in TB case detection and reaching individuals missed by the health system. Once finalized, the PPM national action plan should be adopted with high-level clearance and commitment from key stakeholders, such as the National TB Program (NTP) leadership, Director of Disease Control, and, if possible, the Health Secretary or Minister of Health. The strategies and financial tables from the plan should be integrated into the country’s TB national strategic plan, donor proposals, and national budgeting processes. Finally, the consultation process should result in a draft plan ready for dissemination to key stakeholders for feedback.
